> I’m checking the exact hole-generation modules and the intended interface definitions. The screenshot appears to show two different legacy assumptions: blind screen insert bores and a four-corner removable-plate pattern.
</details>

Those are both deliberate legacy assumptions, but they do not match what you appear to expect.

The angled screen’s six holes per side are **4 mm × 7 mm blind insert bores**, not through-holes. The 7 mm screen-face rail exists specifically to hold those blind M3 inserts, with no nut access behind it. That is why the holes stop and why the rail looks thick. See [the rail and cut definition](./designs/cyberdeck-2/src/parts/enclosure_blockout.scad:59) and [the 7 mm configuration](./designs/cyberdeck-2/configs/rev_0001.json:28).

If the screen should bolt through into the main chamber, the correct replacement is a 3.6 mm through-hole through the angled rail, with an internal nut/washer pocket and actual driver/nut installation access. The rail can then be reduced toward the 3 mm structural minimum except where a dedicated fastener land needs more material.

The flat top “2U” plate likewise has only **four** M3 positions—one at each corner—because it was modeled as a removable cover, not as a full rack-pattern interface. The code explicitly generates only `2 × 2` holes. [See the loop](./designs/cyberdeck-2/src/parts/enclosure_blockout.scad:221).

A proper 2U rack-style top interface would use the canonical six-hole pattern on each side: 12 holes total. The current 14 mm rails can support that pattern: at the standard `X = ±118.2625 mm` positions, the narrowest opening-side ligament is about 3.46 mm after a 3.6 mm hole—just over the 3 mm minimum.

Do you want the plan updated to make both interfaces use through-bolted 12-hole 2U patterns, with internal nut/driver access for the screen and the top plate?

> propose a detailed fix for all of these issues i mentioned

The fix should be one coordinated rebuild of the screen interface, upper roof lock, and top plate—not separate patches.

| Area | Correct fix |
|---|---|
| Screen 2U rails | Replace the 7 mm blind-insert bores with 3.6 mm through-holes. Reduce the broad rail to a 3 mm structural face flange; bolts pass from the screen side into the main chamber, with accessible M3 nut/washer pockets on the chamber side. Keep the canonical six-hole pattern per side. |
| Screen “thick wall” | The current thickness is solely to retain 7 mm blind inserts. Once through-bolting is used, retain only 3 mm continuous rail and side-wall material, plus local 3 mm-backed nut lands if needed. No long 7 mm solid wall should remain. |
| Raised screen roof join | Add an 18 mm minimum service band above the unchanged 2U screen opening by extending the whole 45° profile, side infills, rear closure, and roof together. Put both halves of the M3 tongue/socket lock inside that band, below the exterior roof and above the screen clearance envelope. |
| Roof-lock hardware | Use a complete station: 3.6 mm passage, top-accessible head seat, chamber-side captive/accessible nut pocket, defined driver path, and at least 3 mm material to every wall, opening, and roof edge. Do not locate the washer recess beside the rear wall. |
| Screen-to-top-opening rail transition | Replace the two rectangular roof cuts plus the overlay bridge with one pre-split 2D opening polygon. The retained side rail expands continuously from 3 mm at the screen opening to 14 mm at the top-plate opening through a named transition length; it is one solid, not two rail ends. |
| Stray nub | First isolate it in a diagnostic crop with the contributing modules separately visible. Then remove its actual owner or replace it with a declared fastener feature. Do not change generic seam hardware until that attribution is proven. |
| Flat top 2U plate | Replace the current four-corner pattern with the canonical six-hole-per-side 2U pattern: 12 total M3 holes, matching the screen and main receiver spacing. Use 3.6 mm through-holes in the plate and roof rails. |
| Top-plate fasteners | Use low-profile M3 button heads rather than 8.25 mm washer recesses at the end holes; the first/last canonical hole center is only 6.35 mm from the 2U edge. Use underside captive-nut pockets oriented so their smallest projected extent leaves at least 3 mm to the plate/opening edges. The 14 mm rail width supports this: `(14 − 6.812) / 2 ≈ 3.59 mm` lateral material around an M3 nut. |

Execution order:

1. Add the diagnostic crops and prove the source of the nub and current rail mismatch.
2. Rebuild the single roof-opening profile and its continuous 3-to-14 mm rails.
3. Convert the angled screen rails to through-bolted, six-per-side mounting rails and reduce the obsolete blind-insert thickness.
4. Add the unified 18 mm upper screen service band and move the roof-lock hardware into it.
5. Convert the top plate and roof rails to the full 12-hole 2U pattern with complete nut/head access.
6. Add explicit post-cut assertions for every hole: exterior edge, opening edge, neighboring hole, nut pocket, tool path, and structural overlap.
7. Run the complete manifest build and full installed assembly review, inspecting the targeted crops before any commit.

This preserves the standard 2U interfaces while making every fastener actually installable and every rail continuous.

Yes. The triangle is the angled-screen side infill, and it is incorrectly solid behind the screen rail holes.

It was added to close and strengthen the side wedge, but the model only cuts the 3.6 mm hole through the angled rail. It does not cut a corresponding nut/head/tool clearance through the new side infill. So the hole is geometrically present yet unusable from the back—exactly what your image shows.

The proper correction is not simply removing the triangle. We should:

- Preserve the outer wedge as structural skin.
- Define the actual screen fastener stack: screw direction, head type, nut or insert location, and driver path.
- Cut a bounded clearance pocket through the infill behind each screen-rail mounting hole, with at least 3 mm remaining material around the pocket and at its support edges.
- Add dedicated section/crop views showing each rear-side mounting station is reachable and unobstructed.
- Update the plan and rebuild/audit the complete artifacts.

> these two rails should meet. That is the strength. This triangle is unhelpful and blocks other clearances. these two rails should just meet and overlap.
>
> also, it looks like only the flat rails on top have the hex stud backing. lets put that backing on all the rails and remove the triangles.
>
> explain in detail how to accomplish this.

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I’ll map the two rail volumes and their attachment coordinates before describing the change, so the overlap is a defined 3 mm structural joint—not another visual near-contact.
</details>

The triangle is the wrong load path. It was added as a side-wedge infill to bridge the angled screen rail and the flat top-opening rail, but it creates a bulky third member inside the space needed for the screen fasteners. The intended strength should come from the two rails themselves meeting with positive overlap.

Here is the correct approach.

1. Replace the triangle with a direct rail-to-rail joint

At each side of the enclosure, the angled screen rail will be extended at its lower/rear root, and the corresponding flat top rail will be extended toward it. Their ends will intersect as solids—not touch at an edge.

The joint will be a named overlap of at least 3 mm in every load-bearing direction:

- 3 mm minimum overlap along the rail’s run.
- Full 3 mm wall thickness through the rail face.
- At least 3 mm of remaining material around nearby holes.

This turns the screen rail and top rail into one continuous structural path at each side. The triangular infills will be removed entirely, including both left and right copies.

2. Preserve the actual 2U clearances

The overlap will occur only outside:

- the angled screen’s 222.25 × 88.90 mm 2U insertion aperture;
- the lower roof opening;
- the top plate opening;
- each rail’s M3 hole and hardware envelope.

The screen’s 45° face angle and its existing aperture stay unchanged. If the rails need to be longer to get a real overlap without invading these clearances, the rail length changes—not the clearance geometry.

3. Give every rail the same M3 through-bolt treatment

You are correct: the flat top rails and main-chamber rails have local hex-nut backing lands, while the angled-screen rails currently only have 3.6 mm through-holes through a 3 mm face.

The angled screen rails will receive the same modeled stack:

- 3.6 mm M3 through-passage through the rail.
- A local backing land behind every hole, following the 45° rail normal.
- A rear-open hexagonal M3 nut pocket in each backing land.
- Enough material behind the nut pocket and around the outer rail edge to retain the 3 mm minimum.
- A defined screw direction: insert from the screen face; nut installs and is tightened from the rear/open side.

These should be separate local lands at each mounting location, not a continuous thick wall. That preserves the clearance behind the screen and avoids recreating the triangle problem.

4. Add structural and serviceability checks

The implementation should add named assertions for:

- each direct rail-to-rail overlap;
- the rail endpoint supports after the triangles are gone;
- M3 hole, hex-pocket, and exterior-edge margins;
- 2U aperture clearance;
- no intersection between a nut/tool envelope and the screen volume or roof opening.

It should also add dedicated section views looking normal to the angled rail, so each of the six M3 stations per rail visibly has a clear hex pocket and tool approach. The review must prove the joint and hardware geometry in the individual printable leaves, not only in the combined STL.

5. Build and review the complete set

After that: complete manifest build, manifest audit, full assembly review, individual-leaf inspection, and combined-STL inspection—then update the plan, validation record, structure report, and journal before committing.

The existing triangle is not needed once the rails have a real overlap, so this is a simplification as well as a clearance fix.

> how do i disable that limit?

You generally can’t disable the tool’s hard per-command limit from the project. But we can avoid it correctly by running the build as a background process, then polling its status and log in short commands until it completes.

For this project, I should use the normal pipeline this way:

```powershell
$job = Start-Process python `
  -ArgumentList 'scripts/scad_build_all.py --design cyberdeck-2 --config designs/cyberdeck-2/configs/rev_0001.json --destination current' `
  -WorkingDirectory 'C:\Users\CJ\Documents\GitHub\vibe-modeling' `
  -WindowStyle Hidden `
  -PassThru `
  -RedirectStandardOutput '.tmp\scad\cyberdeck-2\build.log' `
  -RedirectStandardError '.tmp\scad\cyberdeck-2\build.err'

$job.Id
```

Then poll with `Get-Process -Id <id>` and read the log. Once it exits, run the normal manifest audit and full assembly review. That keeps the canonical build pipeline intact and avoids timeouts without writing artifacts anywhere outside `.tmp/scad/cyberdeck-2/` and `output/cyberdeck-2/`.

> i want to create a vscode launch.json python hook which rebuilds any folders where the design folders have been modified more recently than the corresponding build artifacts. explain how we would do that.

Use a small Python stale-build hook plus a VS Code task. The launch configuration should call the task with `preLaunchTask`; `launch.json` itself should not contain the rebuild logic.

The hook would:

1. Enumerate `designs/*/parts.json` to find governed multipart designs.
2. For each design, identify its intended build config—ideally an explicit field such as `default_build_config` in `parts.json`, rather than guessing among `configs/*.json`.
3. Compare the newest modification time anywhere under `designs/<design>/` against the corresponding `output/<design>/build_manifest.json`.
4. Mark a design stale when:
   - `output/<design>/build_manifest.json` is missing;
   - the output audit fails;
   - any file in `designs/<design>/` is newer than the manifest;
   - optionally, shared geometry dependencies such as `references/engineering/ten_inch_rack/` or shared source libraries are newer.
5. For each stale design, run only the normal complete pipeline:

   ```powershell
   python scripts/scad_build_all.py --design <design> --config <config> --destination current
   ```

6. Immediately run its `--audit-only` mode. The hook exits non-zero if a build or audit fails, preventing the debugger from launching with stale or incomplete artifacts.

A useful command shape would be:

```powershell
python scripts/rebuild_stale_designs.py --all --audit
```

Then VS Code configuration is straightforward.

`.vscode/tasks.json`:

```json
{
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "Rebuild stale CAD designs",
      "type": "shell",
      "command": "python",
      "args": [
        "scripts/rebuild_stale_designs.py",
        "--all",
        "--audit"
      ],
      "problemMatcher": [],
      "presentation": {
        "reveal": "always",
        "panel": "dedicated"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

`.vscode/launch.json`:

```json
{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Run CAD tooling",
      "type": "python",
      "request": "launch",
      "program": "${workspaceFolder}/scripts/your_tool.py",
      "console": "integratedTerminal",
      "preLaunchTask": "Rebuild stale CAD designs"
    }
  ]
}
```

Two details matter:

- Compare against `build_manifest.json`, not an arbitrary STL timestamp. The manifest represents the complete installed build.
- Do not use this hook for source-only previews or partial part builds. It should always call `scad_build_all.py` and let that pipeline atomically replace `output/<design>/`.

Timestamp detection is convenient, but it can miss content changes after a timestamp-preserving operation. A stronger later version can compare the source/config hashes recorded in each `build_manifest.json`; that is more reliable than timestamps while still rebuilding only when necessary.

> ok so this would accomplish what i'm saying in the terminal window whenever i click the play button in vscode, right?

Yes.

When you click VS Code’s play/debug button for that launch configuration, VS Code runs the `preLaunchTask` first. That task invokes the Python hook in the integrated terminal, which rebuilds only stale designs and audits their canonical `output/<design>/` artifacts. Only after it succeeds does VS Code launch the configured program.

If no design folder is newer than its build manifest, the hook prints that nothing needs rebuilding and proceeds immediately.

This is a manageable migration, but `agentic-pipelines` is more than a renamed `agents` repository. It adds a pipeline runtime, prompts, schemas, local-inference configuration, state/evidence conventions, and stricter VS Code entrypoint rules.

I inspected the current repositories:

- Existing submodule: `agents/`, pinned at `e723231c`
- New repository: [`cjtrowbridge/agentic-pipelines`](https://github.com/cjtrowbridge/agentic-pipelines), current `main` at `89d3b3e4`
- Only four host files currently refer directly to `agents`, plus `.gitmodules`, so the path migration itself is small.

The first decision is the local path. Although the repository is named `agentic-pipelines`, its own documentation expects it to be mounted at:

```text
./pipelines
```

I recommend following that convention. Commands and examples throughout the new framework use paths such as:

```powershell
python pipelines/scripts/pipeline.py ...
```

Mounting it at `./agentic-pipelines` would work only if we deliberately maintained host-specific path overrides throughout the documentation and scripts.

## Recommended migration

### 1. Create an atomic migration plan

The plan should explicitly cover:

- current `agents` commit and inventory;
- new `agentic-pipelines` commit;
- submodule replacement and rollback;
- host-policy synthesis;
- path-reference migration;
- optional runtime adoption;
- VS Code entrypoint reconciliation;
- documentation, validation, journal, commit, and push.

This is important because the new repository’s `AGENTS.md` contains universal rules that overlap—but do not perfectly match—this repository’s existing CAD governance.

### 2. Preserve the host policy hierarchy

The root [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md) should remain canonical for this repository.

Its opening policy would change conceptually from:

```text
root AGENTS.md
→ agents/RULES.md as fallback
```

to:

```text
root AGENTS.md
→ pipelines/AGENTS.md for pipeline-specific routing and baseline rules
```

The host must retain its existing CAD requirements, including:

- plan approval;
- structural joins;
- artifact manifests;
- complete-build review order;
- ten-inch-rack rules;
- journal checkpoints;
- no kanban;
- host-owned output conventions.

We should not replace the root policy with the upstream file.

### 3. Replace the submodule

After verifying the old submodule is clean, the controlled Git operation would be approximately:

```powershell
git submodule deinit -f -- agents
git rm -f agents
git submodule add https://github.com/cjtrowbridge/agentic-pipelines.git pipelines
git submodule update --init --recursive pipelines
```

Then pin and record the exact new commit.

The old submodule should not be edited or repointed in place because this is a different repository with a different architecture. A remove-and-add operation produces a clearer Git history and rollback boundary.

### 4. Synthesize affected host files

At minimum, update:

- `.gitmodules`
- root `AGENTS.md`
- `README.md`
- `playbooks/how_to_bootstrap_framework_submodule_into_host_repo.md`
- `playbooks/how_to_update_submodule_and_synthesize_host_overrides.md`

The current direct path references are limited to:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `README.md`
- bootstrap playbook
- create-playbook playbook

We should also create a synthesis report comparing:

```text
old agents baseline
+ current host policy
+ new pipelines baseline
= resulting host policy
```

That report should identify every upstream rule we adopt, override, or defer.

### 5. Separate framework mounting from runtime adoption

We do not need to activate a real agentic pipeline merely to replace the framework submodule.

The first migration can mount `pipelines/` and update governance without immediately creating:

- `pipeline.yaml`
- `api.yaml`
- host prompts;
- runtime state;
- artifact/thread/report directories;
- local Ollama configuration.

Those should be added only when we define an actual pipeline for this repository.

If we do adopt the runtime immediately, we would also need:

- tracked `api.sample.yaml`;
- ignored `api.yaml`;
- `requirements-pipeline.txt`;
- ignored pipeline state, thread, report, and candidate directories;
- a host-owned bootstrap script;
- preflight verification;
- a concrete host pipeline definition.

I recommend deferring runtime activation to a second plan.

### 6. Reconcile VS Code behavior

The new framework requires every declared pipeline entrypoint to have a VS Code task and exactly one primary play action that enters through a host-owned bootstrap script.

We just added a primary play configuration for stale CAD rebuilding. During migration, we must decide whether:

- stale CAD rebuilding remains the primary play action; or
- a future ordinary pipeline operation becomes primary, with CAD rebuilding retained as a task.

We should not silently overwrite the current VS Code configuration during submodule migration. If no host pipeline is activated yet, the CAD rebuild configuration can remain primary.

### 7. Validate the cutover

Before accepting the migration:

- verify the new submodule commit;
- ensure no remaining `agents/` references;
- ensure no accidental legacy `RULES.md` dependency;
- validate plan indexes;
- verify root host precedence remains explicit;
- ensure no kanban artifacts were introduced;
- run the new framework’s relevant validators/tests;
- verify existing CAD commands and artifact policies are unchanged;
- inspect `.gitignore` for pipeline-local credentials and runtime evidence;
- document a rollback procedure.

## Rollback

The migration should be one focused commit. Rolling it back should restore:

- the `agents/` submodule path and pointer;
- the prior `.gitmodules`;
- the prior host-policy routing;
- all prior documentation references.

No host plans, journals, CAD sources, or generated artifacts should be moved into the new submodule, so rollback remains clean.

My recommended scope is: replace `agents/` with `pipelines/`, synthesize governance and documentation, but defer actual pipeline runtime configuration until we have a specific pipeline to build.
